tumor-bearing mice in each group.
Moreover, the anti-tumor immune response was evaluated in vivo. On the
30th day, the mice were euthanized, brain tumor tissues were harvested to
prepare a single cell suspension via the percoll cell isolation solution, the
immune cells were stained and analyzed by FCM in order to evaluate the
overall changes of immune cells within the tumor microenvironment.
Quantitative FCM results showed that after IL-12&VEMR@Gel treatment,
the proportions of mature DC cells (CD80+CD86+), CD8+ T cells
(CD3+CD8+), and the activation of T cells (CD25+CD69+) in the GBM
lesions of tumor-bearing mice were significantly increased, whereas the
proportions of Treg cells (CD4+Foxp3+) and MDSCs (CD11b+Gr-1+) were
notably reduced. This indicated a broad reversal of the immunosuppressive
microenvironment in GBM after injecting IL-12&VEMR@Gel into
intracavity, which was a crucial step to exert an antitumor immunity. Given
that changes in the types and numbers of immune cells in the tumor
microenvironment, which can lead to alterations in cytokine levels,
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was used to evaluate the
expression of relevant cytokines at the tumor site. After treatments, the IL-
12&VEMR@Gel group induced the highest levels of interferon-γ (IFN-γ)
and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), which were closely related to the
anti-tumor effect of CD8+ T cells and the activation of T cells. In contrast,
the levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-10 (IL-10), which are
associated with the maintenance of the immunosuppressive characteristics
of the tumor microenvironment, were the lowest. These results further
confirmed that IL-12&VEMR@Gel comprehensively and thoroughly
activated the anti-tumor immune response within the brain, transforming
GBM from a “cold” tumor to a “hot” tumor.
Taken together, the combination of IL-12 and VEMR is more conducive to
recruiting immune cells, thereby exerting anti-tumor immune effects and
inhibiting the recurrence of GBM.

Critique #7:
Finally, while it is an excellent immunostimulatory cytokine in many other
cancers, IL-12 in GBM has decreased effectiveness in activating T cell
responses in situ due to baseline low proportions of infiltrating T cells in
GBM. The greatest effectiveness of IL-12 has been seen in combination
with other immunomodulators in preclinical studies. Have the authors
considered any other immunomodulators in lieu or in combination with IL-
12?
Response #7:
Thank you for your profound insight into the limitations of IL-12 in GBM
immunotherapy. The suggestion of combined immunomodulators you put
forward is of great value.
Although T-cell infiltration is relatively low in the immune
microenvironment of GBM, IL-12, as a “master regulatory factor”
cytokine, its immune activation effect is not limited to the T-cell population.
Instead, it reshapes the immune microenvironment through multiple
mechanisms and enhances the anti-tumor immune response: (1) IL-12 is a
key regulator of NK cell activation, which can upregulate the expression
of activating receptors (e.g., NKG2D) on NK cells, enhancing their
cytotoxicity against tumor cells [1-4]. (2) IL-12-induced Th1 polarization
increases the production of IFN-γ, which can directly inhibit GBM cell
proliferation and enhance the sensitivity of tumor cells to immune attack
[5-7]. (3) IL-12 can upregulate the expression of CD25 and CD69 on CTLs,
promoting T cell activation and proliferation [1,8-9]. (4) IL-12 can reprogram
M2-type immunosuppressive macrophages into M1-type pro-
inflammatory phenotypes, enhancing their antigen presentation and
phagocytic capabilities, and improving the immunosuppressive
microenvironment [10]. (5) IL-12 can suppress GBM angiogenesis [11], a key
process for tumor growth and progression.
In our research, the immune cells were stained and analyzed by FCM to
evaluate the overall changes of immune cells within the tumor
microenvironment in the recurrence model. Quantitative FCM results
revealed that after IL-12&VEMR@Gel treatment, the proportions of
mature DCs (CD80+CD86+), CD8+ T cells (CD3+CD8+), and activated T
cells (CD25+CD69+) in the GBM lesions of tumor-bearing mice
significantly increased, whereas the proportions of Treg cells (CD4+Foxp3+)
and MDSCs (CD11b+Gr-1+) notably decreased. This finding indicated a
broad reversal of the immunosuppressive microenvironment in GBM after
injecting IL-12&VEMR@Gel into the intracavity, which is a crucial step
in antitumor immunity. Given that changes in the types and numbers of
immune cells in the tumor microenvironment can lead to alterations in
cytokine levels, an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was
used to evaluate the expression of relevant cytokines at the tumor site. After
treatment, the IL-12&VEMR@Gel group exhibited the highest levels of
interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), which are
closely related to the antitumor effect of CD8+ T cells and the activation of
T cells. In contrast, the levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-10
(IL-10), which are associated with the maintenance of the
immunosuppressive characteristics of the tumor microenvironment, were
the lowest. These results further confirm that IL-12&VEMR@Gel
comprehensively and thoroughly activated the antitumor immune response
within the brain, resulting in the transformation of GBM from a “cold”
tumor to a “hot” tumor.

We acknowledge that preclinical studies have shown enhanced
effectiveness of IL-12 when combined with other immunomodulators (e.g.,
anti-PD-1) [12,13]. For example, Chen et al.[12] demonstrated that combining
Nano-IL-12 (i.v.) with anti-PD-1 antibodies (i.p.) enhances anti-tumor
immunity. However, most of these studies focus on primary tumor, while
our study specifically targets recurrent GBM—a setting with distinct
biological features. Herein, following your recommendation, we further
combined the widely used immune checkpoint inhibitor anti-PD-1 in
CT2A postoperative resection recurrence model. The results showed that
the combination of anti-PD-1 (IL-12&VEMR&PD-1@Gel) did not
significantly inhibit tumor growth compared with IL-12&VEMR@Gel.
Fig. 14. (A) Luminescence images of orthotopic Luc-CT2A GBM tumor-bearing mice
following different treatments monitored on day 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. (B) Quantified
signal intensity of (A). (C) Survival analysis of orthotopic Luc-CT2A GBM tumor-
bearing mice in each group.
We hypothesized that this lack of synergy is due to the unique
microenvironment of recurrent GBM: (1) GICs are pivotal drivers of
recurrent GBM. Their inherently low expression of MHC-I and co-
stimulatory molecules renders them invisible to cytotoxic T cells,
conferring natural resistance to adaptive immunity [14]. IL-12 breaks this
evasion by unleashing multifaceted antitumor programs. (2) The IL-
12&VEMR@Gel group achieved almost complete tumor clearance
especially in the GL261 post-treatment recurrence model, only IL-
12&VEMR@Gel can fully activate anti-tumor immunity and achieve
excellent therapeutic effects by employing the “elimination of GICs and
reshaping the microenvironment” dual mechanism. At this point,
combining other regulators no longer provides additional therapeutic space;
instead, it would increase the complexity of the drug combination and the
treatment cost, thereby burdening the patients more and being unfavorable
for clinical application.
As previously mentioned, GICs play a critical role in recurrent GBM,
which are resistant to conventional therapies and are the main source of
tumor recurrence [15,16]. These suggested that modulating immunity alone
is insufficient to inhibit recurrent GBM, while targeting and eliminating
GICs is essential. Thus, we combined IL-12 with VEMR (a strategy
targeting both glioma cells and GICs, inhibiting GICs stemness and killing
GICs/glioma cells). The results showed remarkable synergistic effects. The
fewest tumors were present and the longest survival time were monitored
in the IL-12&VEMR@Gel group compared with IL-12@Gel group and
VEMR@Gel group. These suggested that IL-12 has already been
combined with VEMR to inhibit recurrence by employing the “elimination
of GICs and reshaping the microenvironment” dual mechanism.
In summary, our study has two key advantages. First, we fully utilized the
multi-faceted mechanisms of IL-12 (activating NK/CTL cells, inducing
Th1 polarization, reprogramming macrophages, inhibiting angiogenesis)
to overcome the low baseline T cell infiltration in GBM, and experimental
results confirmed its effective immunostimulatory effects. Second, we
focused on the unmet clinical need of recurrent GBM, recognizing that
GICs are the core driver of recurrence. By combining IL-12 with VEMR
(targeting GICs), we addressed both the immunosuppressive
microenvironment and the root cause of recurrence (GICs), achieving
superior anti-tumor efficacy compared to monotherapies. This strategy
provides a novel and promising approach for treating recurrent GBM.

Critique #1:
What the authors are proposing is a complex combination of particular
agents and molecules and the choice of each was not based on strong
rationales or experimentation. For example, GRP78 was used to target
with dVAP, but whether GRP78 is indeed highly and selectively expressed
on GBM cells or GICs was not presented. MIT was chosen but there could
be other chemotherapeutics that can be locally delivered to kill GICs and
why particularly MIT is unclear. It felt that the authors just picked up
agents and molecules what they like to test and put them together. Scientific
basis or rationale is weak.
Response #1:
We sincerely appreciate your meticulous review and insightful comments
on our manuscript. We apologize for any lack of clarity in the Abstract and
Introduction regarding the selection rationales of the agents used in our
research. However, we would like to emphasize that these choices were not
arbitrary but based on careful consideration and prior knowledge.
(1) Regarding the use of GRP78 targeted by DVAP:
GRP78, a specific cancer cell-surface marker, is implicated in cancer cells
proliferation, apoptosis resistance, metastasis and drug resistance. Beyond
its intracellular functions, GRP78’s presence on the cell surface and its role
in the tumor microenvironment underscore its potential as a therapeutic
target. There were numerous reports indicating that GRP78 protein
overexpressed on both glioma cells and GICs [1,2]. Recent studies have
explored innovative strategies to target GRP78, including small molecule
inhibitors [3], monoclonal antibodies [4], and chimeric antigen receptor
(CAR) T cell therapy [5], showing significant potential in glioma treatment.
To provide a more intuitive demonstration, we characterized the expression
levels of GRP78 through Western blot, the results showed that all four
glioma cell lines (CT2A, GL261, U251, U87) exhibited high expression of
GRP78.

(2) Regarding the choice of mitoxantrone (MIT):
Temozolomide (TMZ) is the primary chemotherapeutic agent for GBM,
but at least 50% of the patients develop resistance to treatment [7, 8].
Acquired resistance to TMZ seems to be the main reason for the short
median survival of GBM patients. TMZ, a DNA methylating agent, exerts
its effect by methylating the guanine base, interfering with the DNA
replication and repair processes [9]. However, tumor cells can easily
develop resistance to TMZ by upregulating DNA repair mechanisms, such
as the expression of O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase (MGMT),
which is the most well-known resistance mechanism [10,11]. In contrast, the
unique structure of MIT enables it to incorporate into the DNA double
strands, inhibiting the activity of topoisomerase II, thereby hindering the
function of DNA [12]. This mechanism of action is not easily affected by the
common drug resistance mechanisms of tumor cells. Especially when
dealing with tumor cells that are resistant to TMZ, it can effectively
overcome the MGMT-mediated resistance problem and continuously exert
the effect of killing tumor cells.
And the second reason, evidences demonstrated that MIT exerts cytotoxic
effects on GICs approximately 50-fold greater than TMZ and surpasses the
efficacy of other agents such as trifluoperazine and pyrvinium pamoate [13],
which is more applicable to the recurrence model. Moreover, MIT can
induce GBM to expose calreticulin (CRT) and release ATP [14], activating
dendritic cell antigen presentation, forming a “chemotherapy-immunity”
synergy with IL-12, while the ICD effect of TMZ is significantly weaker.
(3) Regarding the choice of siNotch1:
Notch signaling, as an important mediator, is associated with self-renewal
and therapeutic resistance of stem cells, and evidence has been found that
Notch1 is overexpressed in GICs, which has a critical role in maintaining
GICs stemness [15]. The stemness of GICs can lead to immune escape. This
is because GICs express low levels of major histocompatibility complex
class I molecules and co-stimulatory molecules, which reduces their
recognition and killing by immune cells [16]. By knocking down Notch1 via
small interfering RNA (siRNA), we aimed to disrupt the stemness of GICs,
thereby enhancing their susceptibility to chemotherapy and immune-
mediated killing.
In summary, the combination of these agents was carefully designed.
Targeting GRP78 with DVAP allows for specific delivery of drugs to both
glioma cells and GICs. MIT was chosen for its superior efficacy against
GICs compared to TMZ. Knocking down Notch1 helps to eliminate the
immune-evasive property of GICs by reducing their stemness. The overall
treatment strategy achieved a significant improvement in inhibiting the
growth and recurrence of GBM in our research.

of GIC markers. Several studies showed that, in addition to Notch1,
GICs also exhibit several other stemness markers, including CD133,
Nestin, BMI1, OLIG2, Oct4, Sox2, CD44, etc[1-2]. We fully recognized the

characteristics of GICs. Therefore, in our research, U87 GICs were

Critique #14:
Page 13, Line 1:“lysosomes were labeled with LysoTracker (green),…”
lysotracker marks any acidic pH, therefore, it is not labeling only
lysosomes but also endosomes.
Response #14:
Thank you for your meticulous review of the experimental details. The
question you raised regarding the range of LysoTracker labeling is
extremely crucial. LysoTracker is a fluorescent dye that selectively stains
acidic compartments within living cells. The pH of the early endosomes is
close to neutral, while the pH of the late endosomes is close to that of
lysosomes (late endosomes pH 5.0-6.0, lysosomes pH 4.5-5.0). Therefore,
theoretically, lysotracker should be able to label the late endosomes and
lysosomes. We used LysoTracker to label the acidic compartments, aiming
to track the distribution of drugs within the cells. However, we failed to
clearly distinguish between endosomes and lysosomes, which was an
oversight in the experimental description. Thus, we change the expression
of “lysosomes” to “lyso/endosomes”.
Although the LysoTracker labeling range covers endosomes and lysosomes,
we inferred the escape path of the MIT and siRNA through the analysis of
the time course. High colocalization of siRNA/MIT with LysoTracker at 2
h, suggesting that the drugs have entered the acidic compartments. The
colocalization coefficient significantly decreased at 8 h, and the
fluorescence signal diffused from the acidic compartments to the
cytoplasm (Figure 4D). This dynamic change conforms to the temporal
characteristics of “endosome-lysosome escape”. The results indicated that
most of the siRNA and MIT entered the lyso/endosomes and then escaped
from the lyso/endosomes over time.

multiple groups were assessed by one-way ANOVA. A p-value of less than
0.05 was considered statistically significant (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p <
0.001, ****p < 0.0001). We have now explicitly defined these in the Section
4.16 to ensure transparency.
Critique #19:
Page 15, Figure 5- Panels G and H are blurry and not very clear.
Response #19:
Thank you for pointing out the clarity issues of Figures 5G and H. We have
reprocessed the original data of this figure to ensure that the image
resolution and contrast meet the publication standards. The scratch images
at 0h, 12h, and 24h were processed using the Image J. The cell migration
rate was calculated by measuring the width of the scratches. However, we
realized that since GICs are usually in a semi-adherent state, using cell
scratch assays to characterize the migration of GICs is not entirely reliable.
After much consideration, we have decided to delete the data related to cell
scratch experiments.
Fig. 44. (A) Scratch assay of U87 cells incubated with PBS, MIT, VE, VER, VEM and
VEMR for 0h, 12h and 24 h. (B-C) Quantification of relative migration distance for
12h (B) and 24 h (C). (D) Scratch assay of U87 GICs incubated with PBS, MIT, VE,
VER, VEM and VEMR for 0h, 12h and 24 h. (E-F) Quantification of relative migration
distance for 12h (E) and 24 h (F).
Critique #20:
Page 16, Line 6: Note that murine GL261 (should be stated in the text that
they are murine inoculated into immunocompetent mice as immune
profiling is required), unlike the human U87 cell line, this line is known to
be far less invasive than actual GBM cells.
Response #20:
Thank you to the reviewers for pointing out the limitations of the GL261
model in simulating the invasiveness of human GBM. Based on this
recommendation, we revalidated the therapeutic effect of IL-
12&VEMR@Gel using a CT2A mouse glioma cell line (derived from
C57BL/6 mice, significantly more invasive than GL261) that is closer to
the clinical GBM characteristics. The relevant data have been
supplemented to the Section 2.5 (Figure 7G-I). We investigated the
therapeutic effect of this multifunctional exo-gel delivery system on CT2A
orthotopic glioma model. Luciferase-expressing CT2A (Luc -CT2A)
glioma cells were implanted into brains on day 0, and mice underwent
imaging using IVIS to determine the glioma growth. On the 6th day after
inoculation with Luc-CT2A cells, the brain tumor was surgically removed.
The mice were randomly divided into four groups, and a multifunctional
exo-gel delivery system was injected into the resection cavity. The results
showed that IL-12&VEMR@Gel significantly inhibited tumor growth and
prolonged the survival of mice. Taken together, these results demonstrated
the excellent ability of IL-12&VEMR@Gel in suppressing glioma
recurrence.
Fig. 45. (A) Luminescence images of orthotopic Luc-CT2A GBM tumor-bearing mice
following different treatments monitored on day 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. (B) Quantified
signal intensity of (A). (C) Survival analysis of orthotopic Luc-CT2A GBM tumor-
bearing mice in each group.
Critique #21:
Page 17- Figure 6: quantitative analysis should be performed on the IHC
slides following staining of relevant markers: proliferation, apoptosis,
immune-profiling, and angiogenesis … .and not only H&E and
measurement of fluorescence/bioluminescence.
Response #21:
Thank you for your suggestions on the depth of immunohistochemical
analysis. We fully agree with the importance of quantitative analysis for
mechanism elucidation and conducted quantitative analysis of H&E and
TUNEL staining. The relevant results have been supplemented to Section
2.5, Figure S15. H&E staining results showed that there was no significant
difference in the proportion of tumor-bearing brain regions between the
Control group and the Gel group, and the proportions in the EM@Gel,
EMR@Gel and VEMR@Gel groups decreased further significantly.
Notably, the fewest tumors were displayed in the IL-12&VEMR@Gel
group among all groups (Figure 7E, Figure S15A). Additionally, extensive
ap extensive
apoptotic cells were detected in TUNEL-stained tumor-bearing brain slices
of IL-12&VEMR@Gel group compared with other groups (Figure 7F,
Figure S15B).
Fig. 46. (A) Representative H&E images of the orthotopic GBM tumors after the
indicated treatments. (B) TUNEL staining of brain tissue sections obtained from mice
tumors after treatments. (C) Quantification of tumor area in H&E images. (D)
Fluorescence quantification of TUNEL assay.
Critique #22:
Discussion, page 22, lines 3-5: there are several newer treatments
approved by the FDA and EMA that can and should be mentioned, such as
TTF (optium), immunotherapies/vaccines (gliovac), oncolytic virus, etc...
Response #22:
Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We have added in the Discussion
the latest approved treatments by the FDA and EMA, as follow: “The
standard clinical therapeutic approach for GBM involves surgical removal
of tumors, after which TMZ treatment and/or radiation therapy are
administered following a several-week recovery interval. In addition,
emerging adjunctive therapies such as tumor electrical field therapy (TTF),
Gliovac™, and oncolytic viruses are used to treat GBM. Nevertheless,
incomplete surgical removal of the tumor, resistance to chemotherapy and
radiotherapy, poor patient compliance and limited targeting ability for
postoperative microscopic residual TTF lesions, the small scale of clinical
trials for Gliovac™, and systemic inflammatory toxicities of oncolytic
viruses all contribute to the difficulty in curing GBM.” (Page 16, Line 21-
26，Page 17, Line ,1-3)
We believe that compared with these emerging therapies, our approach
offers several decisive advantages. (1) TTF interferes with the mitosis of
tumor cells through alternating electric fields, offering a non-invasive
modality with negligible systemic toxicity [1]. However, the limitations of
TTF include the need to wear the device continuously (for at least 18 hours
per day), poor patient compliance, and limited targeting ability for
postoperative microscopic residual lesions. Our approach is free from such
compliance burdens and is designed to reach and eradicate residual disease
that TTF cannot effectively target. (2) Gliovac (an anti-GBM vaccines in
clinical trial) can induce specific T-cell responses by loading tumor-
associated antigens (TAAs) [2,3]. However, profound inter-patient
heterogeneity prevents any single vaccine from covering all cases. Our
system circumvents this limitation because it does not rely on predefined
antigens; it not only induces T cell infiltration but also reduces M2-type
macrophages and inhibitory cells such as Tregs. Compared with vaccines,
it is more adaptable to the immunosuppressive microenvironment of GBM.
(3) Oncolytic viruses (such as DNX-2401, for diffuse intrinsic pontine
glioma in clinical trial) selectively lyse tumor cells and trigger antitumor
immunity, but viral replication can provoke systemic inflammatory
toxicities [4,5]. In contrast, our system is designed for local release, thereby
virtually eliminating the risk of systemic side effects.
References:
[1] KHAGI S, KOTECHA R, GATSON NTN, et al. Recent advances in Tumor
Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy for glioblastoma[J]. Oncologist, 2025,
30(2):oyae227.
[2] SCHIJNS VE, PRETTO C, DEVILLERS L, et al. First clinical results of a
personalized immunotherapeutic vaccine against recurrent, incompletely resected,
treatment-resistant glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) tumors, based on combined
allo- and auto-immune tumor reactivity[J]. Vaccine, 2015, 33(23):2690-2696.
[3] ZHAO S, QU Y, SUN Z, et al. Glioblastoma Cell Lysate and Adjuvant
Nanovaccines via Strategic Vaccination Completely Regress Established Murine
Tumors[J]. Adv Healthc Mater, 2025, 14(14):e2500911.
[4] PHILBRICK B, ADAMSON DC. DNX-2401: an investigational drug for the
treatment of recurrent glioblastoma[J]. Expert Opin Investig Drugs, 2019,
28(12):1041-1049.
[5] NASSIRI F, PATIL V, YEFET LS, et al. Oncolytic DNX-2401 virotherapy plus
pembrolizumab in recurrent glioblastoma: a phase 1/2 trial[J]. Nat Med, 2023,
29(6):1370-1378.
Critique #23:
Line 7: The ”cold” TME in GBM is there, to begin with, prior to any
surgery and treatment. Moreover, this is also a result of the treatments
themselves as the radiation and chemo both harm the immune system. It
may be worth thinking about how the treatments suggested in the paper
can be combined with a general busting of the immune system to improve
the outcomes.
Response #23:
Thank you to the reviewers for pointing out the inherent attributes of “cold
TME” in GBM and the immunosuppressive issues of traditional treatments.
The core innovation of this study lies precisely in breaking through the
immunosuppressive limitations of traditional radiotherapy and
chemotherapy through the dual strategy of local immune activation and
tumor stem cell targeting. Locally delivered IL-12 could activate tumor
immunity, while MIT induced immunogenic cell death (ICD), and the two
synergistically reverse “cold TME”. Mechanically, the damage-related
molecular patterns (DAMPs) released by MIT form a positive feedback
with the IL-12-activated Th1-type immune response, rather than the
immunosuppression of traditional chemotherapy.
Available data suggest that IL-12&VEMR@Gel can reshape the local
immune microenvironment of the surgical remnant. Immunofluorescence
showed that the infiltration of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells and mature DC
cells in the brain tumor tissues of the IL-12&VEMR@Gel treatment group
was significantly higher than that of the control group.
Fig. 47. (A) The CD4+ T cells、CD8+ T cells、DC cells in tumor-bearing brain tissues.
(C-E) Quantification of CD4+ T cells (B), CD8+ T cells (C), DC cells (D).
Moreover, quantitative FCM results (Figure 8B-F) showed that after IL-
12&VEMR@Gel treatment, the proportions of mature DC cells
(CD80+CD86+), CD8+ T cells (CD3+CD8+), and the activation of T cells
(CD25+CD69+) in the GBM lesions of tumor-bearing mice were
significantly increased, whereas the proportions of Treg cells (CD4+Foxp3+)
and MDSCs (CD11b+Gr-1+) were notably reduced. In conclusion, the IL-
12&VEMR@Gel system has initially improved the inherent and
chemotherapy-induced “cold” TME defect of GBM through the synergistic
effect of ICD and IL-12.
Figure 48. The evaluation of antitumor immune response in GL261 postresection
glioma-bearing brain tissue. (A) Schematic diagram of the experimental design. (B)
Representative FCM contour plots of T cells in each group and quantification of CD8+
T cells. (C-F) Quantification results of the proportion of DC cells (C), T cell activation
(D), Treg cells (E), and MDSCs (F) in tumor-bearing brain issues of each group.
Critique #24:
Page 23, Line 5: safety was not addressed in the non-malignant healthy
brain tissue.
Response #24:
Thanks for the reviewers’ comments. Regarding this, we would like to
make the following responses: Firstly, we investigated the targeting ability
of DVAP-exosome (VE) in U87 cells, U87 GICs (GRP78 positive) and
HA1800 cells (GRP78 negative), proving that the fluorescence signals of
VE on normal cells was significantly lower than that on tumor cells. This
result suggests that when the system targets GRP78, non-specific damage
to healthy brain tissue may be significantly reduced. Further, we also
evaluated the targeting of non-glioma and non-GIC brain cells (neurons,
astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia). We compared the uptake of Exo,
VE, and VEMR in HT22, BV2, HMC3 and MO3.13. Exosomes were
labeled with CM-DiI and then incubated with different cell lines. Among
the three types of cells, there was no statistically significant difference in
the fluorescence intensity of the four groups.
Moreover, the survival time of mice in the IL-12&VEMR@Gel treatment
group was prolonged longer than 180 days in GL261 model (Figure 7D),
and no neurological dysfunction symptoms (such as dyskinesia, epilepsy,
etc.) occurred, indirectly reflecting the limited damage to the brain
parenchyma caused by local administration.
Fig. 49. (A-B) In vitro cellular targeting of Exo, VE, VEMR, DVAP peptides+VE in
HA1800 cells (A) and U87 cells (B). (C) Quantification of targeting in HA1800 cells
and U87 cells.
Fig. 50. (A-D) In vitro cellular targeting of Exo, VE, VEMR, DVAP peptides & VE in
HT22 cells (A), BV2 cells (B), HMC3 cells (C), MO3.13 cells (D), U87 cells (E) and
U87 GIC (F). (G) Quantification of targeting in different cells.
Critique #25:
Page 24, line 1-6- a much more comprehensive analysis should be done in
order to claim that the tumor growth inhibition was achieved by turning
the cold TME into a hot one.
Response #25:
Thank you for your meticulous review and valuable suggestions on our
research. Your suggestion that the mechanism verification of “cold TME
transforming into hot TME” requires a more comprehensive analysis of
immune cells is crucial for deepening the mechanism explanation in this
article and we fully concur with this perspective. On the 30th day, the mice
were euthanized, brain tumor tissues were harvested to prepare a single cell
suspension via the percoll cell isolation solution, the immune cells were
stained and analyzed by FCM in order to evaluate the overall changes of
immune cells within the tumor microenvironment, including Treg cells
(CD4+FoxP3+), MDSCs (CD11b+Gr-1+), DC (CD80+CD86+), effector T
cells (CD45+CD3+CD8+), T cell activation (CD25+CD69+). Given that
changes in the types and numbers of immune cells in the tumor
microenvironment, which can lead to alterations in cytokine levels,
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was used to evaluate the
expression of relevant cytokines at the tumor site, including IFN-γ, TNF-
α, IL-4 and IL-10. The relevant results have been supplemented to Section
2.5, Figure 8.
IFN-γ is predominantly secreted by Th1 cells and NK cells and serves as
the signature cytokine of Th1-type immunity. It enhances macrophage
phagocytosis and microbicidal activity, accelerates dendritic-cell
maturation, up-regulates MHC-molecule expression, and thereby
potentiates cell-mediated immunity. Its concentration thus mirrors the
magnitude of the Th1 immune response. TNF-α, chiefly secreted by
macrophages and T cells, is a pivotal pro-inflammatory cytokine that
initiates the inflammatory cascade, activates immune effector cells, and
potentiates anti-tumor immunity. IL-10 is a potent immunosuppressive
cytokine produced by Treg and Th2 cells, macrophages, and other cell
types. It restrains the activation of Th1 cells, macrophages, and dendritic
cells, reduce the release of pro-inflammatory factors, and maintain immune
balance. Increased IL-10 expression is a hallmark of immunosuppressive
microenvironments. In our research, compared with the control group, the
concentration of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-4, and IL-10in the Gel group and
EM@Gel group did not show any significant change. The levels of IFN-γ
and TNF-α were significantly increased in VEMR@Gel, IL-12@Gel, IL-
12&VEMR@Gel group, whereas IL-4 and IL-10 were reduced to varying
extents. Notably, the IL-12&VEMR@Gel group induced the highest levels
of IFN-γ and TNF-α, while the levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and
interleukin-10 (IL-10) were the lowest.
The proportions of CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells in different treatment
groups were detected by flow cytometry. The proportions of CD4+ T cells
in different treatment groups (Control, Gel, EM@Gel, EMR@Gel,
VEMR@Gel, IL-12@Gel, IL-12&VEMR@Gel) were 7.83%, 5.76%,
9.18%, 11.88%, 13.36%, 12.91%, 16.18% respectively, while the
proportions of CD8+ T cells were 10.58%, 11.17%, 22.36%, 22.75%,
24.27%, 26.37%, 37.16%. Compared with the control group, the
proportions of CD4+ T cells and CD8+T cells in the Gel group showed no
significant changes. In the other group, the proportions of CD4+T cells and
CD8+T cells all increased. Among them, the proportion of CD4+ T cells
and CD8+ T cells in the IL-12&VEMR@Gel group increased significantly.
This indicates that the combined treatments of IL-12 with VEMR can
promote the proliferation of CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells.
Compared with the control group, the proportion of DC cells in the Gel
group showed no significant difference. In the EM@Gel group, EMR@Gel
group, VEMR@Gel group, IL-12@Gel group and IL12&VEMR@Gel
group, the proportion of DC cells increased to varying degrees. Especially
in the IL-12&VEMR@Gel group, the proportion of DC cells increased to
10.3%. The results showed that combined treatment can promote the
proliferation of DC cells.
CD25+CD69+ is the classic marker of T cell activation. Compared with the
gel group (Gel), there was no significant difference in the proportion of
CD25+CD69+ T cells between the control group and the gel group; the
proportions of CD25+CD69+ T cells in the EM@Gel group, EMR@Gel
group, VEMR@Gel group, IL-12@Gel group and IL-12&VEMR@Gel
group were significantly higher than those in the control group. The
increase in the proportion of double-positive cells indicates that these
treatments may exert immunomodulatory effects by enhancing T cell
activation.
Regulatory T cells (Treg) are a subset of T cells with immunosuppressive
functions, which can promote tumor progression by suppressing the anti-
tumor immune response in the tumor microenvironment. Therefore, by
marking FoxP3, it is possible to specifically identify and quantify Treg
cells. Compared with the gel group (Gel), there was no significant
difference in the proportion of Treg between the control group and the gel
group. In the EM@Gel group, EMR@Gel group, VEMR@Gel group, IL-
12@Gel group and IL-12&VEMR@Gel group, the proportion of Treg
gradually decreases. IL-12&VEMR@Gel group demonstrated the lowest
level, which was 3.4%.
Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) is also a type of cell population
with significant immunosuppressive functions. The combined labeling of
CD11b and Gr-1 can effectively distinguish MDSC from mature myeloid
cells and other immune cells, and is currently a standardized method for
identifying MDSC. Similar to Treg cells, combined administration of IL-
12 and VEMR can significantly reduce the proportion of MDSC.
To sum up, after IL-12&VEMR@Gel treatment, the proportions of mature
DC cells (CD80+CD86+), CD8+ T cells, and the activation of T cells
(CD25+CD69+) in the GBM lesions of tumor-bearing mice were
significantly increased, whereas the proportions of Treg cells (CD4+Foxp3+)
and MDSCs (CD11b+Gr-1+) were notably reduced.
These results further confirm that IL-12&VEMR@Gel comprehensively
and thoroughly activated the anti-tumor immune response within the brain,
transforming GBM from a “cold” tumor to a “hot” tumor.
Figure 51. The evaluation of antitumor immune response in GL261 postresection
glioma-bearing brain tissue. (A) Schematic diagram of the experimental design. (B)
Representative FCM contour plots of T cells in each group and quantification of CD8+
T cells. (C-F) Quantification results of the proportion of DC cells (C), T cell activation
(D), Treg cells (E), and MDSCs (F) in tumor-bearing brain issues of each group. (G-J)
ELISA quantification results of IFN-γ (G), TNF-α (H), IL-4 (I), and IL-10 (J) in tumor-
bearing brain issues.
The above is our point-by-point response to the reviewer's comments.We
sincerely appreciate the dedicated work of the editors and reviewers and
hope that the changes will be recognised. Once again, thank you very much
for your comments and suggestions. If you have any questions, you can
contact me at any time at your convenience.
Many thanks!
Best Regards,
Yours truly,
Prof. Huining He

Ocular Diseases, School of Pharmacy, School of Biomedical Engineering
and Technology, Tianjin Medical University.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have done a thorough job of addressing the previous concerns. As it stands, the manuscript is substantially improved and should be considered for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This revised manuscript has been improved due to new data derived from additional experiments that have conducted during the revision. However, I still note some remaining weaknesses as listed below.
1. “This one-month post-operative interval represents a crucial period during which tumor recurrence often occurs.” This statement is not true. GBM recurrence typically occurs about 8-10 months after the initial surgery and after post-operative chemoradiation therapy. Relapse can occur earlier but rarely happens within the first one month.
2. Exos release from the gel was shown in Figure S2. However, I have not found that the authors showed whether IL-12 encapsulation into the gel was feasible and IL-12 can be released from the gel. Since IL-12@gel was effective in suppressing GBM growth (Figure 7), apparently gel encapsulation of IL-12 was feasible, but it would be nice to show the basis for this.
3. What was exactly the IL-12 that was used in this work? Recombinant mouse IL-12? This should be clarified in the Materials and Methods section.
4. In the Result description of Figure 6D and G, the authors did not recognize that survival and tumor suppression were comparable in the IL-12 and IL-12&VEMR groups.
5. The results description of Figure 7 (Section 2.5) perhaps should be split into two paragraphs for the GL261 part and the CT2A part.
6. I suggest that description of Figure 8 could be a separate section, 2.6.
7. Also consider re-structuring section 2.1, where the second paragraph is very lengthy. The part starting with “Gel and VEMR@Gel were subsequently prepared…” could be a new paragraph.
8. Abstract. siNotch1 should be siRNA for Notch1.
9. What siNC is in Figure S7 was not explained in the figure legends.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors addressed properly and thorouly all the concerns.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-point responses to the Reviewers’ comments for Ref:
NCOMMS-24-61002B
Dear reviewers,
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to all reviewers for their
rigorous, professional, and constructive comments on our revised
manuscript. Your valuable feedback has been instrumental in refining the
quality, accuracy, and clarity of our work, and we greatly appreciate the
time and effort you have dedicated to evaluating our study.
First, we are particularly encouraged by Reviewer #1 and Reviewer #3’s
recognition that we have addressed previous concerns thoroughly and that
the manuscript has been substantially improved to be considered for
publication. Additionally, we have carefully reviewed each of Reviewer
#2’s 9 points and have taken targeted actions to address them, including
correcting inaccurate statements, supplementing key experimental
evidence, clarifying reagent details, optimizing result structure, and
refining terminology. Below, we provide a point-by-point response along
with explanations of the revisions made to the manuscript.
Once again, we thank all reviewers for their invaluable contributions to
strengthening our study. We believe the revised manuscript now meets the
high standards of the journal, and we look forward to your further
evaluation.
Response to Reviewer's comments:
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for their
time and constructive feedback. We greatly appreciate their approval of
our manuscript and their thoughtful comments, which have been invaluable
in improving the quality of our work.
Critiques From Reviewer #1:
The authors have done a thorough job of addressing the previous concerns.
As it stands, the manuscript is substantially improved and should be
considered for publication.
Response:
Thank you for your positive feedback and for acknowledging the
improvements made to the manuscript. We are pleased to hear that the
revised version meets your expectations and are grateful for your
recommendation for publication.
Critiques From Reviewer #2:
Critique #1:
"This one-month post-operative interval represents a crucial period during
which tumor recurrence often occurs," This statement is not true. GBM
recurrence typicaly occurs about 8-10 months after the initial surgery and
after post-operative chemoradiation therapy. Relapse can occur earlier but
rarely happens within the first one month.
Response #1:
Thank you for your meticulous review of the manuscript. We have revised
the statement “This one-month post-operative interval represents a crucial
period during which tumor recurrence often occurs” to “This one-month
post-operative interval represents a crucial period during which tumor
recurrence may be triggered” (Page 2, Line 23-24, Section 1).
We also have reviewed recent clinical studies and systematic reviews. We
agreed that 8~10 month period after surgery is the peak time for GBM
recurrence, and also a large number of clinical studies have shown that
GBM can also exhibit rapid early progression (REP) in the early
postoperative period (≤1 month), which has a significant impact on
prognosis. Merkel et al. found that in 61 newly diagnosed GBM patients,
59% developed new enhancement foci or residual tumor progression
approximately 24 days (within one month) after surgery[1]. Waqar et al.
reviewed and pointed out that approximately half of the GBM patients
experienced macroscopic visible REP between surgery and radiotherapy
and chemotherapy, and this was significantly associated with a decline in
survival[2]. These all indicated that the early progression of microscopic
residual tumor cells could eventually drive clinical recurrence in the post-
operative period.
Reference:
[1] MERKEL A, SOELDNER D, WENDL C, et al. Early postoperative tumor
progression predicts clinical outcome in glioblastoma-implication for clinical
trials[J]. J Neurooncol, 2017, 132(2):249-254.
[2] WAQAR M, TRIFILETTI DM, MCBAIN C, et al. Early Therapeutic Interventions
for Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma: Rationale and Review of the Literature[J].
Curr Oncol Rep, 2022, 24(3):311-324.
Critique #2:
Exos release from the gel was shown in figure S2. However, I have not
found that the authors showed whether IL-12 encapsulation into the gel
was feasible and IL-12 can be released from the gel. Since IL-12@gel was
effective in suppressing GBM growth (figure 7), apparently gel
encapsulation of IL-12 was feasible, but it would be nice to show the basis
for this.
Response #2:
We appreciate you pointing out this missing experimental basis of IL-12
encapsulation into the gel and its release behavior in the manuscript.
For IL-12 encapsulation feasibility, as described in the revised manuscript,
during preparation, we first mixed the hydrogel matrix at room temperature
to maintain its liquid state, then added IL-12 to the liquid gel. Since no
phase transition occurs at room temperature, IL-12 is uniformly dispersed
within the liquid matrix without precipitation or leakage. Upon transfer to
37°C, the gel solidifies instantly, trapping all IL-12 within its network
structure, without loss. Figure 2K can prove the viewpoint that all materials
can be polymerized and form gels.
Figure 1. The temperature sensitive properties of Gel at 4 ℃ and 37 ℃.
For characterization of IL-12 in vitro release behavior, we supplemented
in vitro release experiments as follows. IL-12 was marked with Cy3 and
loaded into the gel. Using artificial cerebrospinal fluid as the release
medium, and 3D layer scanning was carried out with a laser confocal
microscope at 0 h and 24 h, respectively. The fluorescence quantitative
results demonstrated that ~86% IL-12 could be released from the gel in 24h,
which was consistent with the release results of the exosomes.
Figure 2. The release of IL-12-Cy3 from the hydrogel in the CSF. (A) 3D layer scanning of IL-12-
loaded hydrogel at 0 h and 24 h. (B) Quantification of the fluorescence intensity in (A).
Critique #3:
What was exactly the IL-12 that was used in this work? Recombinant
mouse 1L-12? This should be clarified in the Materials and Methods
section.
Response #3:
Thank you for pointing out the lack of clarity regarding the IL-12 used in
our study. To address this clearly, we have supplemented the details of the
IL-12 used in all related experiments in the revised "Materials and
Methods" section. The IL-12 utilized was recombinant murine IL-12
(Protech Systems Co., Ltd., USA).
Critique #4:
In the Result description of Figure 6D and G, the authors did not recognize
that survival and tumor suppression were comparable in the IL-12 and IL-
12&VEMR groups.
Response #4:
Thank you very much for your valuable comment on the result description
of Figure 6D and G. After receiving your comment, we immediately
provided additional explanations for the results.. Notably, although the
therapeutic efficacies of IL-12 and IL-12&VEMR were comparable in the
primary-tumor model, in the postoperative resection model, IL-
12&VEMR@Gel exhibited a markedly amplified antitumor effect than of
IL-12@Gel in both GL261 and CT2A recurrent model, underscoring the
pivotal contribution of GICs to recurrence. Our results further confirmed
that IL-12-mediated immune activation alone is insufficient; thus, direct
and specific elimination of GICs becomes indispensable for GBM
recurrence.
Critique #5:
The results description of Fiqure 7 (Section 2.5) perhaps should be split
into two paragraphs for the GL261 part and the CT2A part.
Response #5:
Thank you for this constructive suggestion. We have now divided the
original single paragraph describing Figure 7 (Section 2.5) into two
separate paragraphs: the first focuses on the GL261 data and the second on
the CT2A data.
Critique #6:
I suggest that description of Figure 8 could be a separate section 2.6.
Response #6:
Thank you very much for your valuable suggestions. We have made
adjustments to the structure of the manuscript according to your
suggestions.
Critique #7:
Also consider re-structuring section 2.1, where the second paragraph is
very lengthy, The part starting with "Gel and VEMR@Gel were
subsequently prepared..." could be a new paragraph.
Response #7:
Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have re-structured Section 2.1
by splitting the original lengthy second paragraph. The text starting with
“Gel and VEMR@Gel were subsequently prepared …” now begins a new
paragraph.
Critique #8:
Abstract. siNotch1 should be siRNA for Notch1.
